title: Policies for Long-Run Growth
short: Policies that build physical capital, skills and technology shift LRAS and the PPC outward.
trouble: Students think any boost to demand raises long-run growth. Spending that only shifts AD does not raise potential output unless it adds to the economy's capacity to produce.

blocks.html: Productivity and Growth drives long-run growth, and growth shows up as rightward shifts of LRAS and outward shifts of the PPC. Which policies can speed it up?

Policies that build physical capital, human capital and technology, or that improve the institutions that support them, raise potential output: they shift LRAS (and the PPC) outward. Policies that only raise spending shift AD; they do not raise potential output unless they add to the economy's capacity to produce.

Potential output depends on what the economy has to work with and how well it uses it. A tax rebate spent on consumer goods raises demand for a while, but leaves the economy with the same machines, skills and ideas. Building a port does both: the construction spending raises AD now, and the finished port lets firms produce and ship more later. Economists broadly agree on the sources of growth; they debate which particular policies deliver them best and at what cost.

blocks.name: ec-adas
blocks.cap: Growth shifts LRAS and SRAS right together. Turn on "Spending grows too" to see the usual case, where AD grows along with capacity.

blocks.name: ec-ppc
blocks.cap: The same growth as an outward shift of the production possibilities curve.

blocks.title: Demand or capacity?
blocks.q: Classify: (a) more funding for engineering schools; (b) a temporary rise in consumer confidence; (c) a new highway network.
steps: (a) More human capital: LRAS shifts right.
(b) More spending, no new capacity: AD only.
(c) Construction spending raises AD now; the highways add capital, raising LRAS later.

blocks.title: Growth of potential output
blocks.q: Policies raise productivity growth to 2% a year, and hours worked grow 1% a year. About how fast does potential output grow?
steps: Potential output = output per hour × hours.
Growth $\approx 2\% + 1\% = 3\%$ a year: LRAS shifts right about 3% each year.

blocks.html: Thinking any boost to demand raises long-run growth. Spending that only shifts AD does not raise potential output unless it adds to the economy's capacity to produce. Check: after the spending is over, does the economy have more capital, skills or ideas?
